strengths: Introduces the first anytime NAS benchmark and framework tailored to tabular data, including a new benchmark dataset (NAS-Bench-Tabular) with 160,000 architectures fully trained across three real-world datasets, which is a valuable resource for the community.

Conducts a thorough empirical study of nine existing zero-cost proxies on tabular data, an area that was previously unexplored, and provides useful negative/positive findings (e.g., NTK-based proxies transfer poorly to tabular DNNs).

Proposes ExpressFlow, a new zero-cost proxy grounded in a theoretical connection to synaptic saliency and neuron-wise aggregation, with reasonably rigorous derivations relating it to trainability and expressivity, and demonstrates consistently higher SRCC than prior proxies across three datasets and even reasonable transfer to image NAS benchmarks.

The two-phase filtering-refinement design with a budget-aware coordinator is a sensible and practical way to combine cheap training-free evaluation with more reliable training-based evaluation under a strict time budget, and the formalized objective (Eq. 2) gives an interpretable way to allocate budget.

Extensive appendices provide ablations (initialization, batch size, recalibration weights, data-agnostic property), sensitivity analysis of M/K and U, noise-robustness checks, and additional baselines (warmup/move-proposal combinations, one-shot/weight-sharing NAS), which substantially strengthen the empirical case.

Reports large empirical speedups over RE-NAS/TabNAS while matching or exceeding global-best AUC, and the anytime property (completing search within seconds while improving with more budget) is demonstrated across three datasets.
weaknesses: The search space is a very simple 4-layer fully-connected MLP with only per-layer width choices; it does not include richer architectural elements common in tabular DNN literature (e.g., attention, embeddings, feature interactions, residual connections), which limits how representative the benchmark and search results are of realistic tabular architecture design choices.

The headline claim of 'up to 82.75x' speedup is not representative of all settings — the Diabetes dataset only shows a 1.75x speedup, and the abstract/framing emphasizes the best case rather than giving a balanced picture of variability across datasets.

Baseline comparisons for the full ATLAS pipeline are limited to RE-NAS and TabNAS; other modern tabular NAS or hyperparameter optimization approaches (e.g., BOHB-based full pipelines, more recent transformer/attention-based tabular NAS) are not included as end-to-end anytime baselines, making the significance claim relative to the broader field harder to assess.

The coordinator's key ratios (M/K≈30, U=2) are tuned empirically per benchmark and it is unclear how sensitive/generalizable these settings are to different search space sizes, dataset scales, or hardware, raising reproducibility/generalization concerns beyond the three studied datasets.

Only three tabular datasets (Frappe, Diabetes, Criteo) are used for the main NAS-Bench-Tabular and ATLAS evaluation, which is a relatively narrow empirical base for a method claiming general applicability to 'tabular data' broadly.

Some theoretical contribution (ExpressFlow) is an incremental extension/re-derivation of existing synaptic-saliency-based proxies (e.g., SynFlow) via neuron-wise aggregation and recalibration, and while the derivation is clean, the conceptual novelty relative to prior trainability/expressivity proxies is moderate.

Error bars/variance reporting in the main text figures (e.g., Figure 6) are shown as shaded regions but the number of repeated runs and variance sources (search stochasticity, architecture initialization) are not always clearly specified within the main paper.
